body.heading: Try these first
paragraphs: One: what gets wetter the more it dries? Two: what has many keys but cannot open a single lock? Three: what runs but never walks, has a mouth but never talks, and has a bed but never sleeps?

Four: the more of me you take, the more you leave behind — what am I? Five: what has a head and a tail, but no body at all? Give each one a fair minute of thought before peeking; riddles reward the pause.

body.heading: The answers
paragraphs: One is a towel: drying you is exactly what makes it wet. Two is a piano, whose keys make music instead of openings. Three is a river — it runs, it has a mouth where it meets the sea, and it rests in its bed.

Four is footsteps: every step you take leaves another print behind you. Five is a coin, with a head on one side and a tail on the other. Notice the shared trick — each riddle uses an everyday word (bed, mouth, keys) in its second, quieter meaning.

body.heading: Make one of your own
paragraphs: You can build a riddle from any object in the room. Pick something with a part that shares a name with something else — the hands of a clock, the teeth of a comb, the eye of a needle — then describe only the confusing meaning and let your listener untangle it.
Test it on a friend and listen to their wrong guesses with interest: a good riddle makes the wrong answers feel close, and the right one feel obvious the moment it lands.

takeaway: Riddles hide ordinary things behind literal words — once you see the trick, you can build your own from any object in the room.
